current_answer: Factory AI-skill job ads show a large posted-pay gap, not a raise for workers. A Federal Reserve analysis finds broad AI skills in about 11% of U.S. manufacturing ads in late 2025, while explicit generative-AI skills were in under 1%. AI-skill ads advertised about 70% higher average pay than manufacturing ads overall, but different jobs, employers and locations may explain much of that gap. The note does not track hires, accepted wages or layoffs. Separate studies still warn about weaker junior entry in specific samples; a broad U.S. tracker finds no clear economy-wide AI jobs footprint. None predicts your personal outcome.

catalogue_card.question: Are factory AI job ads paying workers more?
catalogue_card.text: AI-skill manufacturing ads show about 70% higher average advertised pay, but a Federal Reserve note does not track hires or worker raises. Explicit GenAI requests remain rare.

summary: Broad AI skills reached about 11% of U.S. manufacturing ads in late 2025; explicit generative-AI skills remained under 1% through July 2026.
AI-skill ads showed about 70% higher average advertised pay than manufacturing ads overall. This unadjusted comparison is not a raise or causal AI premium.
Separate narrow junior-entry warnings and broad U.S. jobs measures still use different outcomes; none predicts individual risk.
uncertainty: The manufacturing note measures online ads, not completed hires, accepted pay, layoffs or a causal AI effect.
AI-skill pay gaps may reflect occupation, employer, location and changing wage-reporting coverage.
Junior hiring and broad-market studies cover different populations and cannot provide personal odds.
